sm: Hosts Kyle Peterson, Joe Sternberg and Zach Kessel discuss the fallout from Tuesday's Democratic midterm wins, with Democrats at 253 House seats and 54 Senate seats, not counting Alaska and Mississippi where they lead. President Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff, with Wiles moving to the Trump political operation. Sternberg notes Wiles had health issues, but worries Miller, architect of the aggressive immigration roundups that put off voters, signals a doubling down on unpopular policies. Kessel says Trump governs through executive orders and likely will not change course. They also discuss a stock market dip, which Sternberg ties to doubts about the AI investment boom and to Democratic strength in states like Texas, where AI regulation is made.

Sternberg says the strong, broad-based jobs report is backward-looking, while markets worry about AI investment and how new politics might affect it. The hosts then turn to judicial nominations. Senator Chuck Schumer told the Associated Press that Democrats will not allow a right-winger on the Supreme Court, which suggests no Trump nominee would be confirmed in the next two years. Justice Alito is 76 and Justice Thomas is 78, and Kessel thinks Republicans may not win the Senate again until 2032, while Peterson says it might be 2034, given the 2028 map. Sternberg urges against despair, since voters are volatile and both parties tend to overreach, and Peterson adds that Trump is term limited, so the Republican standard bearer is unknown.

Kessel explains why John Ossoff is already discussed as a 2028 Democratic contender: he won by almost twenty points, and his record on Israel aids may help him. The group then plays Ron DeSantis saying no one in the party has Trump's brand, so the party must be ideas based. Sternberg agrees that charisma-based politics is volatile, and Kessel says ideas could reduce the chaos voters disliked. Peterson warns Democrats about the progressive wing, citing Abdul El-Sayed's Medicare for All pitch and ballot measures in Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio on taxes and voter ID. A Third Way write-up found El-Sayed, Peggy Flanagan and Troy Jackson ran about five points behind their party's statewide House vote, and Sternberg expects the activist base to over-interpret the results.
